# What NOT To Do

Hard-won lessons from real failures. Load this when starting any Forge implementation task. Violations here have caused production bugs, CI failures, or hours of wasted debugging.

## Never Do These (Will Break Things)

### 1. Edit generated files

Files under `frontend/src/lib/forge/` (SvelteKit) or `frontend/src/forge/` (Dioxus) are generated by `forge generate`. Any manual edit gets overwritten. If the generated output is wrong, fix the Rust source or the codegen, not the output.

### 2. Hand-write PG trigger SQL for reactivity

Call `SELECT forge_enable_reactivity('table_name');` in migrations. The function creates the trigger, channel subscription, and notification payload. Writing your own trigger SQL will silently break change detection because the payload format won't match what the Reactor expects.

### 3. Trust `#[serde(skip)]` to hide fields from codegen

`forge generate` reads the Rust AST directly, not serde attributes. A `#[serde(skip)]` field still appears in generated frontend types, causing `DESERIALIZATION_ERROR` at runtime. Create a separate `PublicUser` struct without sensitive fields and use that in return types.

### 4. Reuse a ForgeClient across auth state changes

The SSE session binds to a principal on first connection. Toggling the token on an existing client causes `SESSION_PRINCIPAL_MISMATCH`. Destroy and recreate the client when auth identity changes (Dioxus: keyed remount via `use_auth_key()`, SvelteKit: SSE auto-reconnects on `setAuth`/`clearAuth`).

### 5. Call `dispatch_job` or `start_workflow` without `transactional`

The macro emits a compile error if it detects these calls directly. But if you hide them behind a helper function, the compiler won't catch it. Without the transactional attribute, the job inserts happen before the mutation commits. If the mutation rolls back, orphan jobs execute against non-existent data.

### 6. Use `unwrap()` or `expect()` on mutex locks in production code

A single panicking thread poisons the lock and cascades crashes across the runtime. Use `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` with error-level logging. This is enforced across all Forge runtime mutexes.

### 7. Call `refetch()` after mutations on reactive queries

SSE pushes updates automatically when data changes. Calling `refetch()` doubles the network traffic and can cause flicker. The only exception is after workflow step completion in tests, where SSE timing is unreliable.

### 8. Put `#[derive(...)]` before `#[forge::model]`

The model macro must be the first attribute. Derives placed before it interfere with the macro expansion and produce confusing compiler errors.

### 9. Name functions with the macro type suffix

`heartbeat_daemon` generates `HeartbeatDaemonDaemon`. Just name it `heartbeat`. The generated struct adds the suffix automatically: `HeartbeatDaemon`.

### 10. Use `tokio::sleep` for long waits in workflows

Workflows survive restarts. `tokio::sleep` doesn't. After a restart the sleep resets to zero. Use `ctx.sleep()` which persists the wake time in the event store. The macro warns at compile time if it detects `tokio::sleep` > 100s.

### 11. Reuse the authenticated ForgeClient for refresh calls

The `refresh` mutation is `public`, but the ForgeClient still sends the expired access token in the `Authorization` header. The runtime validates the token before checking if the endpoint is public. Use an anonymous `ForgeClient` (no token provider) for refresh calls. `ForgeAuthProvider` (Dioxus) and `auth.svelte.ts` (SvelteKit) handle this correctly.

### 12. Call `logout` inside `with_auth_error_handler` (Dioxus)

Logout triggers a keyed remount which destroys the refresh timer. The user gets logged out before proactive refresh ever fires. Signal a refresh attempt instead, let the refresh logic decide whether to logout.

## Avoid These (Will Waste Time)

### 13. Explore broadly before reading the task surface

Read `forge.toml`, `Cargo.toml`, `src/main.rs`, and the specific files you'll touch. Stop there. Broad exploration burns context and rarely reveals anything the task needs.

### 14. Iterate through trial-and-error on known failure patterns

If `cargo check` or `forge check` fails, load `references/troubleshooting.md` first. Most compilation failures fall into documented categories (SQLX_OFFLINE, struct visibility, ForgeConn borrowing, Docker paths). Don't guess.

### 15. Skip `forge generate` after changing backend contracts

New queries, mutations, models, or enum changes require regeneration. The frontend will compile against stale types and fail at runtime with cryptic deserialization errors.

### 16. Claim completion without running tests

`forge check` validates structure and linting. It does NOT test behavior. Run actual handler tests, and run `forge test` if UI changed.

### 17. Kill processes on occupied ports

If `lsof` shows the port is taken, tell the user and stop. Don't kill the process, change ports silently, or try alternative ports. The user's dev server or another Forge instance might be running intentionally.

### 18. Add `public` to endpoints by default

Auth is required by default for a reason. Every `public` endpoint is an attack surface. Only add `public` when the business requirement explicitly calls for unauthenticated access.

### 19. Use `SELECT *` in subscribed queries

Column-aware invalidation only works when queries list specific columns. `SELECT *` falls back to table-level invalidation, which triggers unnecessary re-fetches on unrelated column changes.

### 20. Write manual identity comparisons

Don't compare `input.user_id != ctx.require_user_id()`. The router's scope enforcement already validates identity fields (`user_id`, `owner_id`, `subject`, `tenant_id` and camelCase variants) at runtime. Manual checks are redundant and error-prone.

### 21. Mock the database in handler tests

Forge's testing philosophy follows sqlx: test against real databases. `TestQueryContext` and `TestMutationContext` accept real database connections. Mocking hides migration bugs, constraint violations, and query plan issues. Use `IsolatedTestDb` from testcontainers for clean per-test databases.

### 22. Use `ctx.http()` for external calls that might fail

`ctx.http()` has no retry or circuit breaking. Use `ctx.http_with_circuit_breaker()` for anything external. Defaults: 5 failures to open, 30s initial backoff. Without this, a flaky external service takes down your handler.

### 23. Use `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` in migrations

It silently skips creation if a conflicting table from scaffold already exists. Use proper migration versioning and let it fail loud if the table is unexpected.

## Frontend-Specific Don'ts

### 24. Write manual SSE/WebSocket management

Generated stores and hooks handle connection lifecycle, reconnection (exponential backoff, 1s base, 30s cap, 10 attempts), and resubscription. Rolling your own loses all of that.

### 25. Use `$effect` or `use_effect` for data fetching

Reactive stores (`$`-suffixed in Svelte, `use_*_live` hooks in Dioxus) handle the subscription lifecycle. Effects create race conditions, duplicate subscriptions, and memory leaks.

### 26. Enforce auth only on the client

Client-side checks are UX. Backend auth (`require_role`, scope enforcement) is security. Every mutation and sensitive query must validate server-side regardless of what the frontend does.

### 27. Forget `ForgeProvider` in the component tree root

Without it, `getForgeClient()` / `use_forge_client()` returns nothing. Components silently fail or panic. This is always the first thing to check when "nothing works."

### 28. Create a single ForgeClient at app root with token toggling (Dioxus)

The ForgeClient in Dioxus does NOT have a `get_token` prop like SvelteKit's ForgeProvider. The token provider is set at construction time. For auth changes, use `use_auth_key()` to generate a key that forces remount of the ForgeProvider subtree.

### 29. Set refresh timer too close to token lifetime

A 12-minute timer with a 15-minute token leaves only 3 minutes of buffer. Use ~2/3 of the token lifetime. For 15-minute tokens, refresh every 10 minutes. For 1-hour tokens, refresh every 40 minutes.

## Macro-Specific Don'ts

### 30. Use bare `log` flag

`#[forge::query(log)]` doesn't work. Use `#[forge::query(log = "info")]` with a quoted string.

### 31. Forget to register handlers in main.rs

Macros generate the structs and trait impls but do NOT make handlers reachable. Each handler needs a register call in `main.rs`:
- Query: `.register_query::<functions::GetItemsQuery>()`
- Mutation: `.register_mutation::<functions::CreateItemMutation>()`
- Job: `.register_job::<functions::ProcessVideoJob>()`
- etc.

If `auto_register()` is used on `Forge::builder()`, explicit registration isn't needed, but verify it's actually wired up.

### 32. Make handler functions private

`#[forge::query] async fn get_items(...)` generates a private struct. `pub use functions::*` in `mod.rs` won't re-export it. Always use `pub async fn`.

### 33. Pass `Option<()>` or `()` as handler input

If the handler has no business input beyond context, omit the parameter entirely. The macro detects `has_input_args = false` and skips scope enforcement. Dummy inputs trigger unnecessary validation.

### 34. Use FnOnce closures in sequential workflow steps with retry

Sequential steps (`ctx.step("name", || async { ... }).retry(3, ...).run()`) need `Fn`, not `FnOnce`, because the closure may execute multiple times. Parallel steps use `FnOnce` (no retry). The compiler will tell you, but the error message is confusing.

### 35. Put MCP tool code in handler that needs HTTP client

`McpToolContext` has no HTTP client. If you need external API calls, dispatch a job from the MCP tool and let the job handle the HTTP work.
